drills.coachNote: Look at your bishop on d4 — right now the only thing holding it up is your queen on f6, since f6-e5-d4 is one clean diagonal. The moment you play Qe6 you're offering exactly the trade White wants: Qxe6, Rxe6, and now nothing guards d4, so Rxd4 just scoops it up for free — a whole piece gone from a position where you were already slightly better. Instead c5 keeps the tension and hits White's b4 pawn while your queen stays home guarding d4; after c5 Bd5 cxb4 axb4 Rxa2 Bxa2 you're trading down favorably with the bishop never left hanging. Before you trade queens, always check what that queen was quietly guarding.

drills.coachNote: Before you played Bb5, notice your knight on g4 is sitting there completely undefended, with White's queen on g3 staring straight down the g-file at it. Bb5 ignores that, so White simply plays Qxg4+ — and because it's check you're shoved to Kf8, then Qh5 keeps hammering and Bd4 lands with real pressure; you've dropped a whole knight and your king's stuck in the center. The fix was h5: your h-pawn defends g4 directly, so if White grabs the knight you just recapture and stay level. After h5 hxg4 hxg4 f5 Qg5 Rad1 the position stays balanced. Whenever a piece is hanging, ask what's actually attacking it before you look anywhere else on the board.

drills.coachNote: You were completely winning here, but your king on g8 only has the g7 pawn for cover, and the c4-g8 diagonal into it is wide open. Playing g6 does nothing about that — White plays Qc4+, you're forced to Kh7, then g4 kicks your queen off h5 while Qe5 claws back a huge chunk of your edge. You needed Qb5, getting your queen active and ready to trade down or escort your king to safety: Qb5 Kg2 Kf8 Kf2 Qd7 Qc4 walks the king to f8 where it's actually safe. In queen endings, king safety comes before pawn moves — every tempo you don't spend fixing your king is a tempo your opponent spends finding checks.

drills.coachNote: Your king on g6 is in serious danger — White's bishop on c4 aims straight down the c4-f7 diagonal, and the knight on g5 covers f7, which means Bxf7 isn't just check, it's mate: your own knight blocks f6, the g5 knight covers that escape, and the queen on h4 covers h6. Rh8 does nothing about any of that, so White plays Bxf7# and the game just ends, from a position where you were comfortably ahead. Nh5 was the resource — it hits White's queen on h4 with tempo and starts untangling your king, so after Nh5 Qxg4 Qxg5 Qxg5+ Kxg5 g3 you're in a sharp fight but very much alive. When your king is this exposed, scan every square around it for mating patterns before spending a move on anything else.

Qf3+ invites …Qxf3, and after gxf3 the checks dry up entirely while Black's knight hops to f4 and starts making problems. Ne5 keeps it sharp instead: Black must take, Nxe5, and dxe5 recaptures WITH CHECK, then Qxe5 grabs the pawn and your queen is still on for Qf3+ next. When you're winning big against an exposed king, look for the move that keeps queens on, not the one that trades them off.

drills.explanation: Both your queen and rook could capture the knight on f4, but Qxf4 is the right way: it wins the knight while the rook on f8 keeps guarding its partner on e8. Rxf4 abandoned that rook — Qxe8+ snapped it off with check, and after Kh7, Qe6 left White completely consolidated. Taking with the wrong piece cost about six pawns.
drills.title: vs prusten63 (873) — Italian Game
drills.coachNote: Notice your rook on e8 before you touch anything else — its only job right now is guarding the back rank against White's queen on h5. Capturing with Rxf4 solves the loose knight but abandons that job, and Qxe8+ just wins the other rook for free with check since nothing else covers e8. The knight on f4 was hanging to your queen too — Qxf4 makes the same capture while your rook stays put on e8. Same target, completely different consequence: always ask which piece is actually free to leave its post before deciding who does the capturing.

drills.explanation: a6 strikes at White's overextended queenside: after bxa6 Rxa6 your rook enters the game down the a-file, and b5 is met calmly by Ra8. Castling let White play Qe2, hitting your knight on c4 — a piece with no defenders — and you had to scramble with c6 and b5 just to hold it, leaving White a wedge pawn on c6.
drills.title: vs prusten63 (873) — Italian Game
drills.coachNote: Your knight on c4 is a great outpost, but your whole queenside behind it — rook on a8, queen still on d8 — is undeveloped, and White's pawn on b5 is exactly the lever that exposes it. Castling ignores that: White plays Qe2, then c6 rips things open before you've caught up. The move was …a6, hitting b5 immediately — after bxa6 Rxa6 your rook jumps to the open a-file with tempo, and you're creating threats instead of waiting around to get hit by one.

drills.explanation: You were a full piece up and just needed to consolidate. c5 gains space, and the knight calmly reroutes to c6 next with b6 and normal development to follow. Ng4 put the knight on a square covered by White's queen all the way back on d1 — Qxg4 took it for nothing, handing the extra piece straight back.
drills.opening: Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.title: vs Feri206 (798) — Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.coachNote: Trace the diagonal from White's queen on d1 — d1, e2, f3, g4 — completely open, nothing in the way. The instant your knight lands on g4, Qxg4 just wins it outright; no trick needed, nothing of yours even covers that square. Playing …e5 afterward doesn't get the piece back, you're just down a full knight. The move was …c5, grabbing central space and preparing …Nc6 — a normal, solid plan that keeps every piece on the board instead of donating one to a queen sitting on an open diagonal.

drills.explanation: Bxa2 trades off White's light-squared bishop on your terms: after Rxa2 you swing rooks to the e-file with Rae8 and Re6, sitting solidly behind the e5 pawn. Rad8 left the bishops eyeballing each other one move too long — Bh6 came with threats at your king, and after g6, Bxe6 fxe6 left you with doubled, weak e-pawns.
drills.opening: Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.title: vs Feri206 (798) — Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.coachNote: You're winning big, but look at the long diagonal from a2 to e6 — White's bishop on a2 is staring straight at your bishop on e6, and it isn't going anywhere. Rad8 lets White pick the moment: Bh6 comes first, forcing …g6 and loosening your king, and only then does Bxe6 happen — you took cosmetic damage for a trade you could've made yourself. Bxa2 makes that same trade on your own terms: Rxa2 recaptures, but now you follow with Rae8 and Re6, keeping your structure clean. When a trade is coming either way, take it before your opponent can attach strings to it.

drills.explanation: Nxc6 wins a full rook: the knight captures its counterpart and forks the queen on e7 and the rook on d8, so after Qd6 saves the queen, Nxd8 collects the rook and Qxg5 even adds a pawn. a4 instead gave Black time for Nxe5, trading off your monster knight, and after Qxe5 his other knight landed on e4 with real counterplay.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs TheArtifier (833) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Look at both your knights — c5 is hitting Black's knight on c6, and e5 is one jump from the rook on d8 once the queen gets nudged aside. That combination is sitting right there, and a4 just lets it evaporate: Black grabs your loose knight with …Nxe5, and after Qxe5 the other knight lands on e4 with real bite, shrinking your edge fast. Nxc6 was the move — it deflects the queen to d6, then Nxd8 forks the rook, and after Qxd8 Qxg5 you've netted a full rook's worth of material. When two knights are both eyeing undefended targets, cash in before your opponent reorganizes.

drills.explanation: Nxc6 is a fork: from c6 the knight hits both the queen on e7 and the rook on d8, so bxc6 is forced — wrecking the pawn cover in front of the king on c8. Then Qd3 turns on the knight on e4, and after Nxc5 bxc5 you're clearly on top. b5 abandoned the b4 pawn's guard of your c5 knight, and Nxe5 won material — no recapture worked.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs TheArtifier (833) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Before pushing that pawn, look at your knights — the one on e5 is attacked by Black's knight on c6, and the one on c5 is attacked by the knight on e4. Both hanging at once, and b5 ignores it. Black plays Nxe5, and after bxa6 bxa6 the other knight jumps to b3, forking your rook on a1 and your remaining knight on c5 — that's how a comfortable edge turns into lost material. Nxc6 was the answer: your e5 knight grabs the attacker first, and after bxc6 Qd3 you're already hitting the e4 knight too. Two hanging pieces means resolve first, push pawns later.

drills.explanation: Rxf7 forces mate in three: your queen on d5 X-rays g8 so f7 can't really be held, and after Rg7+ Kh8, Rg8 is checkmate — the bishop on f6 seals g7 while the queen on d5 guards g8, so the rook can't be taken. Qg5 instead let Black play Rxf2 and keep the counterplay alive.
drills.title: vs yassine3453 (860) — Englund Gambit
drills.coachNote: You had mate on the board and let it go. Rxf7 with your rook was simply crushing — Black's rook on f8 can't stop it, and next Rg7+ forces Kh8, then Rg8 is mate with your bishop on f6 backing it up. Qg5 throws that away, and the instant you stop pressing, Black's rook on c2 and queen on b2 strike back: Rxf2 tears into your king's cover, and after Qe5 Rf3 that rook is crawling all over your second rank. You went from a forced mate to barely better in a handful of moves. When mate is on the board, calculate the forcing line to the end before reaching for a quieter move.

drills.explanation: Qxc8 wins the rook on c8 outright — Black never dares recapture, since your bishop on f6 and rook on e7 strangle his king; he tries Qb5, and after Re8 he must throw his queen away with Qf1+ Rxf1. Qd5 let a won game slip: Qxa3, and after Qxd4, Qxh3 stripped your king — nearly fifteen pawns of advantage gone.
drills.title: vs yassine3453 (860) — Englund Gambit
drills.coachNote: Look at Black's rook on c8 — nothing defends it, and your queen on c4 can just take it straight down the file. Qxc8 wins a full rook for nothing, and after Qb5 Re8 Qf1+ you're heading into a completely winning endgame. Instead Qd5 slides the queen off that file and lets the rook off the hook — Black's queen on b2 then runs wild, hoovering up pawns with Qxa3 and Qxd4, grabbing h3 too, while the rook doubles in with R7e3, and your +20 advantage melts toward equal. When a piece is hanging with nothing defending it, take it first, before anything fancier.

drills.explanation: The g5 pawn was attacking your bishop on f4, and Nxg5 meets that head-on — the knight is covered by that same bishop, and after fxg5 Bxg5 Black's kingside pawns are stripped while his pieces retreat to passive squares like Nf6 and Nb8 as Qf3 builds pressure. Bf5+ dropped a whole piece instead: e6 blocked the check and hit the bishop, and after Bc2, gxf4 won your dark-squared bishop.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs jatin221272 (817) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Black's pawns on g5 and h5 are already gunning for your bishop on f4, and his king is still stuck on d7 — that's what matters here. Nxg5 cashes in: after fxg5 Bxg5 you've traded a knight for a pawn but blown the kingside open with the king still uncastled, and Nf6 Qf3 keeps the pressure on. Bf5+ looks useful because it's check, but it only saves your g6 bishop — after e6 kicks it back to c2, the g5 pawn simply grabs your other bishop on f4 for free. A check that doesn't threaten anything real just hands your opponent a tempo to fix their real problem.

drills.explanation: Nxg5 was the shot: after fxg5 Bxg5 you get two pawns for the knight and Black's king on d7 is stranded, with Qf3 coming to hit the loose d5 pawn (the simple e4 was strong too). Bf5+ backfired — e6 blocked with tempo, the bishop crawled back to c2, and gxf4 scooped up your dark-squared bishop, which the g5 pawn had been eyeing all along.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs jatin221272 (817) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Black's king is still on d7, never castled — that's the target, not a quiet retreating check. e4 rips the center open right now: even if Black answers gxf4, exd5 blasts the position open with the king stuck in the middle, and Qa4+ next is already unpleasant for him. Bf5+ throws that moment away — it only nudges your g6 bishop to safety, and after e6 Bc2 you've spent two moves retreating while Black still gets to play gxf4 and just wins the piece, no compensation this time. When the enemy king hasn't castled, hunt for the move that blows lines open toward it before reaching for a safe retreat.

drills.explanation: Your knight on e4 was attacked by the d3 pawn, and Nd6 is the safe retreat — White wins the e5 pawn with Rxe5+, but Be7 blocks, Bg6 follows, and you're only down a pawn with pieces coming out. Ng5 ran the knight straight onto the c1-bishop's diagonal: Bxg5 won it outright, and White grabbed e5 with the knight as well.
drills.title: vs Stwilso1 (836) — Ruy Lopez Opening Berlin Defense
drills.coachNote: Look at White's bishop on c1 before dropping your knight on g5 — it hasn't moved yet, but the c1-h6 diagonal is wide open, and g5 sits right on it, completely undefended. Bxg5 just wins the knight for free; there's no fight for it at all. Nd6 was the move instead — it pulls the knight to safety, and even though White then grabs your e5 pawn with Rxe5+, after Be7 Qe2 Bg6 you're still fine with all your pieces on the board. A piece that hasn't developed yet can still see the whole board — always check what an unmoved bishop or rook is already aiming at before you walk into it.

drills.explanation: Your knight on g5 was attacked by the bishop on c1, defended only by your queen along the d8–g5 diagonal — and Be7 blocked that exact diagonal. Bxg5 won the knight, and after Be6, Bxe7 Qxe7 left White a clean piece up. Ne6 just steps to safety; after Qf3 Qf6 Nxc6 Bxd3 the position stays a fair fight.
drills.title: vs Stwilso1 (836) — Ruy Lopez Opening Berlin Defense
drills.coachNote: Your knight on g5 has been hanging to that same bishop on c1 for a whole move now, and Be7 develops a different piece while leaving it sitting there. White finally cashes in with Bxg5, and after Be6 Bxe7 Qxe7 you've lost the knight for nothing — just a piece down. Ne6 was the fix: pull the knight itself off that diagonal and out of danger, and after Qf3 Qf6 Nxc6 Bxd3 the position stays roughly balanced with everything covered. A hanging piece doesn't fix itself just because you didn't address it last move — dealing with it comes before developing anything else.

drills.explanation: Bc7 hits the queen on d8 and grabs a square deep in Black's camp: after Qd7, b6 locks the bishop on c7 permanently, cramping the whole queenside while Ra4 swings the rook toward the action. Your e4 gave Black a free move for Bd7, developing with a hit on the b5 pawn — the same Bc7 idea then came a tempo late, and the queen slipped away to c8.
drills.title: vs slammerman001 (850) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Before committing the center with e4, notice Bc7 was right there — your bishop on f4 jumps to c7 and hits Black's queen on d8 directly, since nothing covers that square. That's a free tempo: Qd7 is forced, then b6 and Ra4 let you keep expanding on the queenside with the queen already shoved off its best square. e4 skips that step, so Black gets to play Bd7 first and takes the sting out of the same idea before you use it. It wasn't losing, just wasteful — when a move threatens something concrete for free, play it before the quieter pawn break, since the break isn't going anywhere.

drills.explanation: Qc5 does three jobs: it confronts the queen on b6, attacks the knight on e7, and keeps the b5 pawn defended. After Qd8, Bd6 piles onto e7, and Bxe7 Rxe7 leaves you in full control of the dark squares. Qc3 left b5 with no defender at all — Bd7 came immediately, and after your too-late Qc5, Bxb5 took the pawn for free.
drills.title: vs slammerman001 (850) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Your b5 pawn is hanging with nothing covering it, and Qc3 ignores that completely. Black plays ...Bd7, aiming down the c8-h3 diagonal, then ...Bxb5 just wins the pawn — your Rfb1 shows up a move too late to matter. That turns a small edge into Black being clearly better, nearly a two-pawn swing. Qc5 was right instead: it attacks the queen on b6, forcing ...Qd8, and your bishop jumps to d6, hitting the rook on f8 and winning tempo before trading on e7. When a pawn's loose, look for the move that also creates a problem for them, not just a neutral square.

drills.explanation: Nf5+ is a fork: it checks the king on g3 and attacks the rook on g7 at the same time. After Kf4 you play Nxg7, winning the rook and flipping the game — roughly twelve pawns of swing. Nb7 instead walked into Rc7+, and after Kd8 the rook simply captured the knight on b7.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.title: vs OdisseoAP (826) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: You're winning big here, and the shot you missed is a fork: ...Nf5+ hits the king on g3 and the rook on g7 in the same move. The king has to move, say Kf4, and ...Nxg7 wins the rook outright. Instead ...Nb7 goes after the bishop on a7 but leaves your own king exposed on c8 — White plays Rc7+, your king's forced to d8, and Rxb7 scoops up the knight for free since nothing defends it there. That one in-between check flips a completely winning position into a lost one, a swing of over 12 pawns. Grabbing a piece is only safe once you've ruled out a check like that.

drills.explanation: Bxg3+ wins a pawn with check, and after the forced Kxg3, Rxd1 scoops the rook — d1 had no defender at all, so you net rook and pawn for the bishop. Rd7 put your rook on a square nothing defends (the knight on c6 doesn't cover d7): Rxd7 took it for free, and after Bd6, bxc6 grabbed your knight as well.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.title: vs OdisseoAP (826) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: You're up +6.3 and completely winning, and the key move is ...Bxg3+: your bishop on f4 takes the pawn on g3 with check, forcing Kxg3, and only then ...Rxd1 wins the rook exchange cleanly. Instead ...Rd7 just slides your rook onto a file White already controls — nothing defends d7, so Rxd7 wins it outright. Worse, White follows with Bd6 and bxc6, grabbing your knight on c6 too. That's a totally winning game becoming a loss in two moves. When a check like Bxg3+ is available, play it first — it changes the board before you commit a piece to a contested file.

drills.explanation: Qxb7+ forces checkmate: the queen grabs b7 and checks the king on e7 along the wide-open seventh rank, Black must block with Qc7, and Qxc7 is mate — your knight on f6 covers the escape squares e8 and d7, and the e5 pawn guards the knight. exd4 was a pawn grab with mate on the board; after Bg7 Black started breathing again.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs pisitto999 (814) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: You're up +20 with a forced mate sitting on the board, and you play the quiet recapture exd4 instead of Qxb7+. That check is the whole idea — the king's stuck on e7, and after the forced ...Qc7 block, Qxc7 is mate, since your knight on f6 seals off its escape squares. exd4 lets Black off the hook: after ...Bg7 the position settles down, and by the time dxc5, ...Qc7, Rd7+ happen, you're still winning but you've handed back over 12 pawns of evaluation for nothing. When you're this far ahead, a check on the board deserves a real look before the automatic recapture — this one happened to be mate in two.

drills.explanation: Rd7+ is a deflection: the queen on c7 has to capture, and Nxd7 then forks the rook on b8 and the bishop on f8 — you've won queen for rook, with Rd1 coming to support the knight. Nd7 tried the fork without the preparation: Bg7 simply stepped the bishop out, nothing was won, and Rd6 got met by Rbc8. The open d-file was the key — use it with check first.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs pisitto999 (814) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: You're up +8.2, and the move that actually cashes in is Rd7+ — it's check, so the queen on c7 has to deal with it immediately, and if she captures with ...Qxd7, Nxd7 wins the queen outright for just a rook. Nd7 looks similar since it forks the rook on b8 and bishop on f8, but it's not check, so Black simply moves the rook away with tempo — ...Rbc8 a move later — and the fork evaporates. You still keep a big edge, but you gave back almost 4 pawns of advantage chasing a fork that couldn't actually collect. The difference is forcing power: a check can't be walked away from, a fork without check often can.

drills.explanation: Your queen on a4 was attacked by the knight on c5 and had to reach safety first — Qa3 does it. The Qh4 attacking idea was right but needed f6 first: after f6 gxf6, Black's own pawn on f6 blocks the e7–h4 diagonal, and only then is Qh4 strong. Played immediately, Qh4 landed right on the e7-queen's diagonal — Qxh4 won your queen on the spot.
drills.title: vs Iamastalemate (860) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: You're already down -4.5 here, and Qh4 makes it worse in the simplest way possible — you're just hanging your queen. From e7, Black's queen has a completely clear diagonal through f6 and g5 straight to h4, so ...Qxh4 just takes it for nothing; nothing you have covers that square. Qa3 was the move instead — it keeps your queen safe and off that diagonal, and after ...Re8, c4, d4, you're still fighting an uphill battle but at least you're still a queen up on the deal. Before you put your queen on a square, trace every diagonal and file running through it — h4 sat right on the e7-h4 diagonal your opponent's queen already owned.
